tips.title: Airbrushing Tip: Thin Your Paint Wisely
tips.text: When airbrushing, it's essential to thin your paint with the correct ratio of paint to thinner. A general rule of thumb is to start with a 1:1 ratio (1 part paint to 1 part thinner). However, for some airbrushes, you may need to adjust this ratio to 1:2 or even 1:3, depending on the viscosity of the paint and the desired effect. Experiment with different ratios to achieve the perfect consistency for your model.

tips.title: Hand Painting Tip: Use a 'Wet-on-Wet' Technique
tips.text: When hand painting, try using a 'wet-on-wet' technique to blend colors seamlessly. This involves applying a layer of paint to the model, allowing it to dry slightly, and then adding additional layers of paint without waiting for the previous layer to fully dry. This technique helps to create subtle, nuanced transitions between colors and can add depth and realism to your model.

tips.title: Primer Tip: Use a High-Gloss Primer for Maximum Adhesion
tips.text: When applying primer to your model, choose a high-gloss primer for maximum adhesion. This type of primer creates a smooth, even surface that allows paint to adhere well and reduces the risk of flaking or peeling. Look for primers specifically designed for scale modeling, such as Tamiya or Vallejo primers, which are formulated to withstand the rigors of paint and handling.

tips.title: Decal Tip: Use a 'Soak-and-Scratch' Method for Perfect Application
tips.text: When applying decals to your model, try using a 'soak-and-scratch' method for perfect application. Apply a small amount of water to the decal and let it soak for a few seconds, then use a credit card or similar tool to gently scratch the decal onto the model. This method helps to prevent air bubbles and ensures a smooth, even application of the decal.

tips.title: Weathering Tip: Use a 'Drybrushing' Technique for Realistic Wear
tips.text: To create realistic wear and tear on your model, try using a 'drybrushing' technique. Dip a drybrush into a small amount of paint, then brush it across the model to create textured, worn areas. This technique is particularly effective for simulating rust, dust, or other types of environmental wear. Experiment with different brushstrokes and paint colors to achieve the desired effect.
